So: `Accepted` → `proposal_accepted` (events.py:84; `proposition` is `None` for a cross-link, `links` non-empty); `Refused` → `proposal_rejected` (events.py:119, `violations` empty for the non-map refusals); `Stopped` → **no event**, only a `TranscriptLine` with `what="stopped"` (transcript.py:194-196). ## 1A. The empirical framing (§3 preamble, lines 47)

> "The empirical picture: scaffolded, retrieval-augmented LLMs approach crowd-aggregate accuracy ([Halawi et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18563)), and LLM *ensembles* are statistically indistinguishable from a human crowd on small question sets ([Schoenegger et al., Science Advances](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adp1528)) — but on a leakage-free, continuously-refreshed benchmark superforecasters still beat the best LLM by Brier 0.068 vs 0.119 ([ForecastBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.19839)), several times the GPT-4→GPT-4o gap. The popular read ([ACX](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/the-ai-superforecasters-are-here)) is that scaffolds are worth about a model generation and finance-adjacent questions are where AI does relatively *best*. Encouraging — but the scaffold is doing the work, not the model."

Numbers with citations: Brier **0.068** (superforecasters) vs **0.119** (best LLM), ForecastBench (arXiv 2409.19839). Qualifier attached: "statistically indistinguishable from a human crowd **on small question sets**"; ForecastBench is "**leakage-free, continuously-refreshed**" — i.e. the author is explicitly weighting the leakage-free benchmark above the parity results.

## 1B. Base rate first, then adjust (§3, item 1, line 51)

> "**Base rate before narrative.** Elicit the reference class and its historical frequency in a *separate call that has not seen the scenario*, then adjust in a second call. Merging them invites representativeness: a vivid chain scores high because it is a good *story*."

Key operational detail: **two separate calls**, and the base-rate call must **not have seen the scenario**. No citation attached to this item (the supporting literature is representativeness/Kahneman, invoked by name only).

## 1C. Conditionals, never joints (§3, item 2, line 52)

> "**Elicit conditionals, never joints.** Ask for `P(B|A)` and `P(B|¬A)`; compute the rest. Humans and LLMs both violate the conjunction rule — a detailed conjunction is judged *more* likely than its own conjunct ([Tversky & Kahneman 1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjunction_fallacy)). A five-step chain at 0.8 per step is 0.33, and the model will call it "very likely" if allowed."

Worked number: **0.8^5 = 0.33** for a five-step chain. Citation: Tversky & Kahneman 1983 (linked to the Wikipedia conjunction-fallacy page, not the paper).

## 1D. Small ensembles, k samples, geometric mean of odds, dispersion (§3, item 3, line 53)

> "**Sample k ≥ 5 times** across prompt variants and ideally two model families, then **aggregate by geometric mean of odds** ([summary](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/sMjcjnnpoAQCcedL2/when-pooling-forecasts-use-the-geometric-mean-of-odds)). **Keep the spread**: dispersion across independent elicitations is a defensible first-order estimate of that parameter's uncertainty, feeding §4 at zero extra cost."

Three separable claims: (a) **k ≥ 5**, varied over **prompt variants** and **ideally two model families**; (b) aggregate by **geometric mean of odds**; (c) **retain the dispersion** as the parameter's uncertainty.

Note on evidentiary status: the geometric-mean-of-odds link is an **EA Forum post** ("summary"), not a peer-reviewed source. **`k ≥ 5` carries no citation** — it is the author's judgement. Median and arithmetic mean are **not discussed anywhere in the document**; geometric mean of odds is asserted as the aggregator without a stated comparison against the alternatives. This is a gap if the parent agent expected a median-vs-geomean-vs-arithmetic argument.

## 1E. Do not extremize (§3, item 4, line 54)

> "**Do not extremize by default.** Extremizing helps for independent human forecasters ([discussion](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/biL94PKfeHmgHY6qe/principled-extremizing-of-aggregated-forecasts)), but LLM samples are highly correlated and chain errors compound multiplicatively. Here it manufactures confidence."

The stated reason extremizing transfers badly: **LLM samples are highly correlated** (violating the independence premise) **and** chain errors **compound multiplicatively**. Citation is again an EA Forum post, and it is cited *for the positive result in humans*, i.e. the document's own recommendation runs against its cited source, on an uncited mechanistic argument.

## 1F. Known LLM pathologies / calibration correction (§3, item 5, line 55)

> "**Correct known LLM pathologies**: RLHF pushes models toward confident-sounding outputs ([Taming Overconfidence in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09724)), and verbalized probabilities cluster on round numbers and avoid the tails. Force explicit `<1%` / `>99%` options; add a per-model recalibration map once questions resolve."

Two concrete mechanisms: **forced `<1%` / `>99%` response options**, and a **per-model recalibration map built from resolved questions**. Citation covers only the RLHF-overconfidence half; the **round-number clustering / tail avoidance claim is uncited inline** (`Just Ask for Calibration`, arXiv 2305.14975, appears only in the source list at line 163, never invoked in the body).

## 1G. Coherence / consistency checks (§3, lines 57–62)

> "**Coherence checks to run automatically** (all cheap, all blocking):
>
> - Marginal consistency: `P(B) ≈ P(B|A)P(A) + P(B|¬A)P(¬A)` vs. a directly-elicited `P(B)`; flag >10pp divergence.
> - Relevance: an edge is justified only if `P(B|A) ≠ P(B|¬A)`. Equal values → delete the edge.
> - Symmetry of dependence: `P(B|A) > P(B)` iff `P(A|B) > P(A)`.
> - Chain sanity: compare the model's *verbal* summary ("highly likely") against the computed number and show the conflict. This is the anti-conjunction-fallacy feature, and a genuinely good product moment."

All four are **blocking**, not advisory. The threshold **>10pp** is uncited/author-chosen. Note the fourth check is framed as both a rigor mechanism and **a product moment** — verbal-vs-computed conflict surfaced to the user.

## 1H. Elicitation units — odds ratios, not probabilities (§2, line 39)

> "**Recommendation: signed log-odds as the default, with leaky noisy-OR and noisy-AND per node.** It handles inhibition, which noisy-OR cannot; elicitation is in odds ratios ("~3× more likely"), which forecasters can produce; each edge's contribution is `wᵢ` in bits, so the inspector gets "this edge moved the target +1.2 bits" free…"

Directly relevant to elicitation design: ask the model for a **signed odds ratio ("~3× more likely")**, not a raw probability. Parameter counts: logistic link = **`k + 1` numbers** (line 37); leaky noisy-OR = **`k + 1` numbers** (line 34); full CPT = **`2^k` rows, 16 numbers at k = 4** (line 32), elicited from "a model that will produce non-monotone, mutually incoherent rows."

Also from §2 (line 41), a constraint on elicited numbers: "**saturation** (clip and warn past ~0.99)."

> "**Monte Carlo over parameters → a band, not a point.** Draw each parameter from its across-sample dispersion (§3.3) ~1,000 times and re-run inference. ~20 lines, and the strongest antidote to false precision: the band visibly widens with chain length, which is the honest lesson."

## 1J. Base rates as leak terms — elicited, never defaulted (§5, line 87)

> "**Structural uncertainty is the dominant error term, and the leak is where it lives.** Every node's "no parents active" probability must be *elicited as a base rate*, never defaulted to zero; a zero leak asserts the LLM's cause list is exhaustive, which it never is. Disclose per graph that the computed number is a lower bound if the enumerated causes are only some of the causes."

> "**Provenance per node and edge**: source URLs with retrieval timestamps, model, prompt version, elicitation method, and the k raw samples *before* aggregation. Without the raw samples you cannot distinguish "the model was confident" from "the models disagreed and we averaged"."

> "**Immutable snapshots.** Every published chain is frozen and timestamped so it can be scored later. A forecast you can silently edit is not a forecast."

Trap 5 — LLM-stated joint probabilities:
> "*Test:* inspect the prompts — is the model ever asked for the probability of a whole path or of the target given the story? Is the displayed path probability computed or generated? **Re-run one edge twice; if the stored number moves, it is a single unaggregated sample.**"

> "*Test:* build a chain ending in a rare, documented event ("S&P 500 falls >20% in a quarter", historically a few percent). With no assumptions applied, is the unconditional endpoint anywhere near that? If it reads 30%, the story is driving the number."

> "*Test:* move one edge from `P(B|A) = 0.6` to `0.45` and see whether the headline conclusion flips. If it does and the UI never flagged that edge as load-bearing, the audit story is broken. **Any figure past two significant digits is theatre.**"

Supported by the cited work:

## 2A. Metaculus — resolvable propositions, conditional pairs, annulment (§1, line 9–11)

> "**Metaculus** — an event is not a phrase, it is a *resolvable proposition*. A question is title + background + **resolution criteria** + fine print + dates, and the criteria are load-bearing: they *"should stand on its own as a set of self-contained instructions"* and supersede the background ([FAQ](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/)). Fine print is a deliberate readability valve; questions pass an [approval checklist](https://www.metaculus.com/help/question-checklist/) before going live, because an ambiguous criterion poisons every forecast attached to it."

> "The relevant primitive is the **Conditional Pair**: "if the Parent resolves Yes, how does the Child resolve?" and "if No?", asked together. In the feed each Parent outcome is an **arrow** and each conditional probability a **bar** — a two-branch fork glyph; in the forecasting UI it is a table, or `IF YES` / `IF NO` buttons opening distribution editors. It exists because *"two forecasters could have the same forecasts… while having very different mental models of their relationship"* ([announcement](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/nQhmiKeYPvFaEZfWc/metaculus-introduces-new-conditional-pair-forecast-questions)). **The gap between branches *is* the causal claim** — the unit of value is P(B|A) − P(B|¬A), not P(B|A). One more detail worth copying: when the Parent resolves, the losing branch is **annulled, not scored**. Counterfactual worlds should be visibly *retired*, never silently deleted."

Map-generation/display takeaways: arrow-per-outcome + bar-per-conditional glyph; table or `IF YES`/`IF NO` buttons; **annul, don't delete** retired branches.

## 2E. Causal-graph / model tools — what they do for map display and evidence (§2, lines 23–27)

Vensim SyntheSim (the strongest cited precedent for edit→see-downstream):
> "The best "change an input, see downstream effects" design in existence is Vensim's **SyntheSim**: it auto-generates a slider for every constant *and* superimposes a live sparkline on every variable **directly on the model diagram**; dragging re-simulates instantly with the pre-drag run **ghosted behind**… Vensim also has **Causal Tracing** — click an outcome, walk backward through its ancestors."

Bayesian-network GUIs (Netica, GeNIe, AgenaRisk, BayesiaLab):
> "Bayesian-network GUIs supply the evidence idiom: each node renders a **bar chart of its marginal inside the node box**; click a state to clamp evidence and every other node's bars jump ([Netica](https://www.norsys.com/netica.html)). GeNIe adds whole-graph **sensitivity shading** against a chosen target — red nodes matter, grey have zero influence — with tornado diagrams as drill-down, while candidly admitting sensitivity analysis *"is essentially an art"* ([GeNIe](https://support.bayesfusion.com/docs/GeNIe/bn_sensitivitybn.html)). AgenaRisk overlays **named scenarios on one chart**; BayesiaLab ranks *which unknown to resolve next* by value of information. But BN GUIs never went mainstream because **CPT elicitation is exponential** — a binary node with *k* binary parents needs 2^k numbers, "costly and error-prone" ([Risk Analysis](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/risa.13772)). Noisy-OR and ranked-node methods cut 2^k to ~2k. **Never make a user fill a 2^k table.**"

Guesstimate/Squiggle, Loopy, Kumu, argument mappers, cross-impact analysis:
> "Guesstimate/Squiggle contribute the best uncertainty input ever designed — `5 to 9` as a single literal, Monte-Carlo'd into a **histogram inside the cell** — with the caution that Squiggle models have a legibility problem and QURI found the space commercially niche. Loopy contributes **propagation-as-animation** — watching a pulse cross an edge with visible latency — plus the warning that causal-loop diagrams are underspecified, so its multi-loop examples are *"somewhere between incomprehensible and dead wrong"* ([MetaSD](https://metasd.com/2017/03/loopy/)). If you animate propagation the semantics must be real, or explicitly labelled illustrative. Kumu supplies the sharpest warning in the survey: system maps are *"prone to proof by intimidation — if something looks thorough it must be accurate"*. Argument-mapping tools fail on **context loss** (C supports B but is irrelevant to A) and **pro-side inflation** — **adding a supporting link is cheap, engaging a critic is expensive** ([LW](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/bHXpbf6jXc4bgyrrp/why-is-argument-mapping-not-more-common-in-ea-rationality)). Predating the LLM framing entirely: **cross-impact analysis** (Gordon & Helmer, 1966) is literally a matrix of "how does event *i* occurring change the probability of event *j*"."

The pro-side-inflation point is the file's central warning about **interactive verbs**: an "add"/"expand" affordance is asymmetrically cheap relative to "challenge," and unless challenge is engineered to be equally cheap, the map inflates.

The popular read ([ACX](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/the-ai-superforecasters-are-here)) is that scaffolds are worth about a model generation and finance-adjacent questions are where AI does relatively *best*. Encouraging — but the scaffold is doing the work, not the model."

Key operational detail: **two separate calls**, and the base-rate call must **not have seen the scenario**. No citation attached to this item (the supporting literature is representativeness/Kahneman, invoked by name only).

## 1C. Conditionals, never joints (§3, item 2, line 52)

> "**Elicit conditionals, never joints.** Ask for `P(B|A)` and `P(B|¬A)`; compute the rest. Humans and LLMs both violate the conjunction rule — a detailed conjunction is judged *more* likely than its own conjunct ([Tversky & Kahneman 1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjunction_fallacy)). A five-step chain at 0.8 per step is 0.33, and the model will call it "very likely" if allowed."

Worked number: **0.8^5 = 0.33** for a five-step chain. Citation: Tversky & Kahneman 1983 (linked to the Wikipedia conjunction-fallacy page, not the paper).

## 2A. Metaculus — resolvable propositions, conditional pairs, annulment (§1, line 9–11)

> "**Metaculus** — an event is not a phrase, it is a *resolvable proposition*. Fine print is a deliberate readability valve; questions pass an [approval checklist](https://www.metaculus.com/help/question-checklist/) before going live, because an ambiguous criterion poisons every forecast attached to it."

> "The relevant primitive is the **Conditional Pair**: "if the Parent resolves Yes, how does the Child resolve?" and "if No?", asked together. In the feed each Parent outcome is an **arrow** and each conditional probability a **bar** — a two-branch fork glyph; in the forecasting UI it is a table, or `IF YES` / `IF NO` buttons opening distribution editors. It exists because *"two forecasters could have the same forecasts… while having very different mental models of their relationship"* ([announcement](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/nQhmiKeYPvFaEZfWc/metaculus-introduces-new-conditional-pair-forecast-questions)). **The gap between branches *is* the causal claim** — the unit of value is P(B|A) − P(B|¬A), not P(B|A). One more detail worth copying: when the Parent resolves, the losing branch is **annulled, not scored**. Counterfactual worlds should be visibly *retired*, never silently deleted."

Map-generation/display takeaways: arrow-per-outcome + bar-per-conditional glyph; table or `IF YES`/`IF NO` buttons; **annul, don't delete** retired branches.

class ContractPayoff(BaseModel):
    """A named contract at a named venue, and which side of it you would take.

    The kind of ending where somebody already sells exactly this claim: a
    prediction-market contract that settles on the same question the claim asks.
    Nothing here says what the contract costs, because that is a live price rather
    than a fact about the map.
    """
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    kind: Literal["contract"] = "contract"
    venue: str = Field(
        description="Where the contract trades, by the venue's own name: 'Polymarket', 'Kalshi'."
    )
    contract_id: str = Field(
        description=("How that venue identifies this exact contract, so a reader can look it up and "
                     "a later step can fetch its price.")
    )
    title: str = Field(
        description=("The contract's question in the venue's own words, so a person reading the map "
                     "can see it is really the same question the claim asks.")
    )
    side: Literal["yes", "no"] = Field(
        description=("'yes' if you make money when the claim comes true, 'no' if you make money when "
                     "it fails.")
    )


class PricePayoff(BaseModel):
    """An instrument you would buy or sell, which way, and how far you expect it to move.

    The kind of ending where no contract asks this question, but something traded
    moves when the answer changes: a futures contract, a ticker, one fund against
    another.
    """
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    kind: Literal["price"] = "price"
    instrument: str = Field(
        description=("The thing you would buy or sell, named the way its venue names it: a ticker, "
                     "a futures contract, one fund against another.")
    )
    direction: Literal["long", "short"] = Field(
        description=("'long' if the position makes money when the claim comes true, "
                     "'short' if it makes money when the claim fails.")
    )
    move: float = Field(
        ge=0.0,
        description=("How far the instrument's price is expected to move if the claim comes out true, "
                     "as a fraction of that price: 0.03 means three per cent. The side is carried by "
                     "`direction`, so this number is never negative.")
    )


Payoff = Annotated[ContractPayoff | PricePayoff, Field(discriminator="kind")]

class ContractPayoff(BaseModel):
    """A named contract at a named venue, and which side of it you would take.

    The kind of ending where somebody already sells exactly this claim: a
    prediction-market contract that settles on the same question the claim asks.
    Nothing here says what the contract costs, because that is a live price rather
    than a fact about the map.
    """
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    kind: Literal["contract"] = "contract"
    venue: str = Field(
        description="Where the contract trades, by the venue's own name: 'Polymarket', 'Kalshi'."
    )
    contract_id: str = Field(
        description=("How that venue identifies this exact contract, so a reader can look it up and "
                     "a later step can fetch its price.")
    )
    title: str = Field(
        description=("The contract's question in the venue's own words, so a person reading the map "
                     "can see it is really the same question the claim asks.")
    )
    side: Literal["yes", "no"] = Field(
        description=("'yes' if you make money when the claim comes true, 'no' if you make money when "
                     "it fails.")
    )


class PricePayoff(BaseModel):
    """An instrument you would buy or sell, which way, and how far you expect it to move.

    The kind of ending where no contract asks this question, but something traded
    moves when the answer changes: a futures contract, a ticker, one fund against
    another.
    """
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    kind: Literal["price"] = "price"
    instrument: str = Field(
        description=("The thing you would buy or sell, named the way its venue names it: a ticker, "
                     "a futures contract, one fund against another.")
    )
    direction: Literal["long", "short"] = Field(
        description=("'long' if the position makes money when the claim comes true, "
                     "'short' if it makes money when the claim fails.")
    )
    move: float = Field(
        ge=0.0,
        description=("How far the instrument's price is expected to move if the claim comes out true, "
                     "as a fraction of that price: 0.03 means three per cent. The side is carried by "
                     "`direction`, so this number is never negative.")
    )


Payoff = Annotated[ContractPayoff | PricePayoff, Field(discriminator="kind")]

48	## 2. The design I recommend
49	
50	### 2.1 The rule that makes the comparison honest
51	
52	> **A model number may be differenced against a market quote only when both range over the same set of worlds — so the edge is computed from the world with *no supposition in force*, and a supposed world can only ever show a conditional payoff.**
53	
54	The smallest shape that enforces it is a **signature, not a guard**. The edge is never computed from "a world"; it is computed by one function that requires the base world as its own argument:
55	
56	```python
57	# katalyst/thesis/edge.py — outside domain/, because it touches a quote (INV-11, ADR-0003)
58	
59	class Quote(BaseModel):                     # what a venue says. Never merged with a model number.
60	    venue: str; contract_id: str
61	    p: float                                # the mid, as a probability
62	    spread: float                           # best offer minus best bid
63	    as_of: date; url: str
64	    source: Literal["fetched", "recorded", "user"]
65	
66	class Edge(BaseModel):                      # built by `priced()` and nowhere else
67	    model: Belief                           # unconditional, owner='model'
68	    quote: Quote
69	    costs: float                            # half the spread plus fees, as a probability
70	    edge: float                             # model.p − quote.p − costs. Signed. May be negative.
71	    break_even: float                       # quote.p + costs — useful even with no quote
72	    mixture: tuple[MixtureTerm, ...]        # every term shown: P(H)·P(c|do H) + (1−P(H))·P(c|do ¬H)
73	
74	class NotComparable(BaseModel):
75	    reason: Literal["conditional_world", "no_quote", "no_contract", "different_question"]
76	    said: str                               # the plain sentence the card prints
77	    break_even: float | None                # still printable when only the quote is missing
78	
79	def priced(base: World, shown: World, claim: PropositionId, quote: Quote | None) -> Edge | NotComparable: ...
80	```
81	
82	`base` and `shown` are two required arguments; there is no way to hand `priced` a branch world alone, and `Edge` has no other construction path. Tests: *agree with the market ⇒ edge reads exactly 0*; *a branch world alone does not type-check*; *a missing quote yields `NotComparable` that still prints the break-even.*
83	
84	The **mixture** is the piece both reviews wanted and neither costed: after *Suppose Hormuz opens*, the card still says *"your supposition makes M1 .61; weighted by the map's own P(H) = .36 against the no-open world's .40, the unconditional number is .47 — that is the one compared with .48."* review/'s worked example, with the engine supplying the terms. It needs only `do(¬A)`, which exists.

86	### 2.2 What a stop-loss honestly is here
87	
88	Four things, kept apart on the card, three of them named differently from today:
89	
90	| Card section | What it is | Who owns it | How it is computed |
91	|---|---|---|---|
92	| **What takes you out** | The events over-represented in the worlds where the stop was touched **first** | computed | `lift(k) = P(k happened before the stop ∣ stop first) / P(k happened)`, Wilson interval on the numerator, suppressed below 200 draws, with the median days between *k* and the stop |
93	| **What to watch** | The claim whose adverse flip hurts the terminal most, **and** resolves before it, **and** is publicly observable | computed | two-directional `sensitivity()` + INV-14's two filters. *Renamed from "invalidation"; it is a watchlist, not a stop.* |
94	| **Your risk exit** | The stop price, the target, the horizon | **the user types them** | never derived |
95	| **Execution** | — | — | We say one sentence: *a stop order's trigger is not its fill price*, and nothing else. |
96	
97	**The smallest thing that is both honest and impressive is "what takes you out".** Forty lines over a boolean mask; the brief's most distinctive sentence answered by computation rather than prose; the one output nobody in the competitive landscape ships. "What to watch" is fifteen lines and is the honest remnant of INV-14. Everything above them — expected shortfall, ruin, drawdown — is cut.
98	
99	**What each needs from the engine.** Only one thing, and it is small:
100	
101	```python
102	# katalyst/thesis/draws.py — the ONLY coupling between the finance layer and the engine
103	class Draws(BaseModel):
104	    day_zero: date; days: int
105	    order: tuple[PropositionId, ...]
106	    when:   NDArray[int]      # (n, claims): the day each claim first became true, −1 for never
107	    weight: NDArray[float]    # (n,): all ones for an exact ancestral sampler
108	```
109	
110	"What to watch" needs **endpoint marginals only** — today's `sensitivity()` gives them. P(stop first) / P(target first) need **event times per world**. The inverse query needs **joint samples with times**. All three come from `when`.
111	
112	`weight` is in the shape from day one so the finance layer is **indifferent to ENGINE's Plan A versus Plan B**: an exact core with an ancestral sampler gives weights of one, a likelihood-weighted sampler gives real weights, and nothing above changes. And `when` is derivable from *today's* engine too — `_draw` already computes `truth[claim] = came_true`, a `(versions, worlds, days)` boolean array, whose first true day **is** `when`. **So stack 05 is not blocked on the engine reformulation**: write it against synthetic `Draws`, test it against synthetic `Draws`, turn it on over whichever engine lands.

260	**D1 — Does `move` get a range, and does it ride with the payoff-`kind` fix?**

263	*In code:* `PricePayoff.move: float` becomes a small frozen `Move(mid, lo, hi)` in `domain/proposition.py`, plus one sentence in the prompt.
264	- **Recommended: add it to `fix/04-payoff-kind-required` now.** That branch already moves the prompt fingerprint, so the Hormuz recording must be remade either way. **Marginal cost: $0 and about 40 lines**, plus one session's delay to that branch. 265	- Alternative: leave `move` a point and put the range on the Position form as a **user** number, labelled. Cost: $0, ~10 lines, and one more place where a model number renders as a confident point.
266	- Worst: add it in stack 05. Cost: **a second paid re-recording** (~$4 and 36 minutes for Hormuz, more if the other three are approved). Do not choose this.
267	
268	**D2 — Drop the path product from `domain/` (`feat/04b-evals` item 3)?**
269	Both reviews say a path product along a route is not a probability of anything when claims share causes. FR-11 (P0) names it by hand.
270	*On screen:* the Verify verdict stops reading *"the multiplied-out likelihood is .07"* and starts reading *"opening moves this ending by 32 points, from a base rate of 40%"*, with the weakest edge named by ablation.
271	- **Recommended: drop it; write total effect in stack 05 instead.** Cost: −60 lines in 04, +30 in 05, and a browser deletion. Amends FR-11.
272	- Alternative: land item 3 as planned and delete it in stack 05. Cost: 60 lines written and then thrown away, plus a P0 requirement that was true for a week.
273	
274	**D3 — Does M1 name a Polymarket contract that actually exists?**
275	The fixture's `contract_id` is an honestly-labelled stand-in (*"brent-below-70-2026-10-31"*). The demo's climax is *"the model says .46, the venue says .48."*
276	*On screen:* the contract title becomes clickable and opens the real market.
277	- **Recommended: spend half an hour searching Polymarket by hand for a live oil or Brent contract, and rewrite M1's claim, `contract_id` and `title` to name it exactly.** Cost: ~30 minutes plus one recorded JSON file. 278	- Alternative: keep the stand-in, mark the quote `source: "user"`, and say on the card *"illustrative contract; no venue quotes this claim."* Cost: nothing, and a reader who checks finds nothing at the other end of the link.

282	- **Recommended: no chapters PR.** One short `spec/thesis/` chapter after PR 3, generated from the docstrings, or nothing. 284

289	- Alternative: keep the wording. Cost: nothing to build and a question nobody can answer in the demo.
290	
291	---
292	
293	## 6. What I did not check
294	
295	- **I made no network call.** I do not know whether a Polymarket contract matching M1 exists today — hence D3. The recorded-quote design is deliberately robust to it not existing, but the demo's headline is not.
296	- **I did not run the frontend, Playwright, `make eval`, or anything that calls a model or costs money**, per the common brief.
297	- **I did not re-run the strike-branch numbers myself** (`apply` is not exported from `domain/branch.py` under that name and I stopped rather than hunt). I relied on `spec/multiverse/propagation.md:456`, which records the engine's own `.46 → .41` and `.43 → .36`.
298	- **I did not measure** how long a 20 000-draw daily path simulation takes over the Hormuz map. I estimate milliseconds in numpy over a `(20000, 45)` float array, but I did not run it. If it is slow, the draw count is the knob.
299	- **I did not verify** that the engine's `truth` array is still shaped `(versions, worlds, days)` end-to-end under every branch — I read `propagation.py:1444-1463` and confirmed the assignment, not the full lifetime.
300	- **I did not read** audit-G (generation) or audit-H (UX) in full, only their finance-adjacent rows; ENGINE, GENERATION and UX analysts cover those.
301	- **I did not price** the browser work beyond a line estimate; audit-H's dock placement is assumed correct without my checking the Inspector's section stack myself.
302	- **Calibration is untested and stays untested.** Nothing in this design validates that the model's probabilities are any good. The card says so; that is all it can honestly do.

## 2. The design I recommend

### 2.1 The rule that makes the comparison honest

> **A model number may be differenced against a market quote only when both range over the same set of worlds — so the edge is computed from the world with *no supposition in force*, and a supposed world can only ever show a conditional payoff.**

The smallest shape that enforces it is a **signature, not a guard**. The edge is never computed from "a world"; it is computed by one function that requires the base world as its own argument:

```python
# katalyst/thesis/edge.py — outside domain/, because it touches a quote (INV-11, ADR-0003)

class Quote(BaseModel):                     # what a venue says. Never merged with a model number.
    venue: str; contract_id: str
    p: float                                # the mid, as a probability
    spread: float                           # best offer minus best bid
    as_of: date; url: str
    source: Literal["fetched", "recorded", "user"]

class Edge(BaseModel):                      # built by `priced()` and nowhere else
    model: Belief                           # unconditional, owner='model'
    quote: Quote
    costs: float                            # half the spread plus fees, as a probability
    edge: float                             # model.p − quote.p − costs. Signed. May be negative.
    break_even: float                       # quote.p + costs — useful even with no quote
    mixture: tuple[MixtureTerm, ...]        # every term shown: P(H)·P(c|do H) + (1−P(H))·P(c|do ¬H)

class NotComparable(BaseModel):
    reason: Literal["conditional_world", "no_quote", "no_contract", "different_question"]
    said: str                               # the plain sentence the card prints
    break_even: float | None                # still printable when only the quote is missing

def priced(base: World, shown: World, claim: PropositionId, quote: Quote | None) -> Edge | NotComparable: ...
```

`base` and `shown` are two required arguments; there is no way to hand `priced` a branch world alone, and `Edge` has no other construction path. Tests: *agree with the market ⇒ edge reads exactly 0*; *a branch world alone does not type-check*; *a missing quote yields `NotComparable` that still prints the break-even.*

The **mixture** is the piece both reviews wanted and neither costed: after *Suppose Hormuz opens*, the card still says *"your supposition makes M1 .61; weighted by the map's own P(H) = .36 against the no-open world's .40, the unconditional number is .47 — that is the one compared with .48."* review/'s worked example, with the engine supplying the terms. It needs only `do(¬A)`, which exists.

### 2.2 What a stop-loss honestly is here

Four things, kept apart on the card, three of them named differently from today:

| Card section | What it is | Who owns it | How it is computed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **What takes you out** | The events over-represented in the worlds where the stop was touched **first** | computed | `lift(k) = P(k happened before the stop ∣ stop first) / P(k happened)`, Wilson interval on the numerator, suppressed below 200 draws, with the median days between *k* and the stop |
| **What to watch** | The claim whose adverse flip hurts the terminal most, **and** resolves before it, **and** is publicly observable | computed | two-directional `sensitivity()` + INV-14's two filters. *Renamed from "invalidation"; it is a watchlist, not a stop.* |
| **Your risk exit** | The stop price, the target, the horizon | **the user types them** | never derived |
| **Execution** | — | — | We say one sentence: *a stop order's trigger is not its fill price*, and nothing else. |

**The smallest thing that is both honest and impressive is "what takes you out".** Forty lines over a boolean mask; the brief's most distinctive sentence answered by computation rather than prose; the one output nobody in the competitive landscape ships. "What to watch" is fifteen lines and is the honest remnant of INV-14. Everything above them — expected shortfall, ruin, drawdown — is cut.

**What each needs from the engine.** Only one thing, and it is small:

```python
# katalyst/thesis/draws.py — the ONLY coupling between the finance layer and the engine
class Draws(BaseModel):
    day_zero: date; days: int
    order: tuple[PropositionId, ...]
    when:   NDArray[int]      # (n, claims): the day each claim first became true, −1 for never
    weight: NDArray[float]    # (n,): all ones for an exact ancestral sampler
```

"What to watch" needs **endpoint marginals only** — today's `sensitivity()` gives them. P(stop first) / P(target first) need **event times per world**. The inverse query needs **joint samples with times**. All three come from `when`.

`weight` is in the shape from day one so the finance layer is **indifferent to ENGINE's Plan A versus Plan B**: an exact core with an ancestral sampler gives weights of one, a likelihood-weighted sampler gives real weights, and nothing above changes. And `when` is derivable from *today's* engine too — `_draw` already computes `truth[claim] = came_true`, a `(versions, worlds, days)` boolean array, whose first true day **is** `when`. **So stack 05 is not blocked on the engine reformulation**: write it against synthetic `Draws`, test it against synthetic `Draws`, turn it on over whichever engine lands.

### 2.3 The ladder — how much finance is enough

**Rung 0 — the smallest complete stack 05** (≈ 620 server lines, ≈ 550 browser, four pull requests, ~4 sessions). Everything the brief's trade clauses need to be honestly met on the Hormuz map with no key: (1) `Quote`, recorded-first, dated on screen, with a "no quote" state and a break-even (A5, A8); (2) the edge, unconditional only, mixture shown term by term (A1); (3) a `Position` the user types, and **first touch** on a daily path built from `when` (A4); (4) **the inverse query by lift** — B6; (5) two-directional sensitivity → the watchlist, INV-14 renamed (A2, A3); (6) **shock as a position stress** — re-run the lens on a branch carrying the user's `Insert`+`Do` and report the P&L difference with **no probability attached**, which is B5 in ~40 lines because the insert machinery exists; (7) **ranked tradeable terminals** — B8, by |edge| where a contract is quoted, else by total effect × move, saying which rule ranked each; (8) sizing from the user's own risk budget, with quartered Kelly at the band's low end as a **greyed ceiling** reading *never size to this*; (9) the card and a declarative export that carries its own refusals.

| Further rung | Cost | What it buys | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Live Polymarket** | ~120 lines, 0.5 session | "Auditable" becomes clickable | **Keep**, as the *last* commit of PR 1, opt-in, recorded file as fallback, never in CI |

**D1 — Does `move` get a range, and does it ride with the payoff-`kind` fix?**
Today a price ending says *"short XLE against SPY, three per cent"* — one number with no range, while every belief on the map carries the range the model stated (decision record 0015). Two recorded answers for the same ticker gave `0.35` and `0.15`.
*On screen:* the card reads *"short XLE vs SPY, 6% (4–9%)"* instead of *"3%"*, and the P&L distribution widens honestly.
*In code:* `PricePayoff.move: float` becomes a small frozen `Move(mid, lo, hi)` in `domain/proposition.py`, plus one sentence in the prompt.
- **Recommended: add it to `fix/04-payoff-kind-required` now.** That branch already moves the prompt fingerprint, so the Hormuz recording must be remade either way. **Marginal cost: $0 and about 40 lines**, plus one session's delay to that branch. Risk: the model already omits payoffs (3 of 23 proposals in the one real recording were rejected for `market_without_payoff`); a nested range may push that rate up.
- Alternative: leave `move` a point and put the range on the Position form as a **user** number, labelled. Cost: $0, ~10 lines, and one more place where a model number renders as a confident point.
- Worst: add it in stack 05. Cost: **a second paid re-recording** (~$4 and 36 minutes for Hormuz, more if the other three are approved). Do not choose this.

**D2 — Drop the path product from `domain/` (`feat/04b-evals` item 3)?**
Both reviews say a path product along a route is not a probability of anything when claims share causes. FR-11 (P0) names it by hand.
*On screen:* the Verify verdict stops reading *"the multiplied-out likelihood is .07"* and starts reading *"opening moves this ending by 32 points, from a base rate of 40%"*, with the weakest edge named by ablation.

- Alternative: land item 3 as planned and delete it in stack 05. Cost: 60 lines written and then thrown away, plus a P0 requirement that was true for a week.

**D3 — Does M1 name a Polymarket contract that actually exists?**
The fixture's `contract_id` is an honestly-labelled stand-in (*"brent-below-70-2026-10-31"*). The demo's climax is *"the model says .46, the venue says .48."*
*On screen:* the contract title becomes clickable and opens the real market.

This is the highest value per minute anywhere in stack 05: it turns the fixture's single biggest honesty weakness into the demo's strongest moment.
- Alternative: keep the stand-in, mark the quote `source: "user"`, and say on the card *"illustrative contract; no venue quotes this claim."* Cost: nothing, and a reader who checks finds nothing at the other end of the link.

**D4 — Stack 05 without a docs-only chapters pull request?**
The roadmap's pattern is chapters first, then code. `spec/thesis/` is five promised chapters and a landing page. A stack is capped at four pull requests, and stack 05 needs all four for code.
- **Recommended: no chapters PR.** One short `spec/thesis/` chapter after PR 3, generated from the docstrings, or nothing. Cost: reverses ADR-0011's working rule (review2 proposes the same freeze for different reasons). Buys: the Thesis dock, which is the difference between a computed answer and a demo.
- Alternative: five chapters first, and the dock slips to stack 06.

**D5 — Is the derived thing a stop-loss, or a watchlist?**
`spec/thesis/README.md:7` says *"That is the stop-loss, and it is derived, not guessed"*, and PRD anti-pattern 11 says *"do not type the stop-loss by hand."* I verified the derivation yields nothing usable on the demo's own fixture: for M1, the only claim resolving before it is B — the thing the thesis is betting on.
*On screen:* the card grows a section called **What to watch** (computed, filtered, with dates) and a separate line **Your stop** which the user types, plus **What takes you out** (computed by lift).
- **Recommended: amend INV-14 and FR-23 to say *watchlist*, and let the user own the stop.** Cost: ~0 lines of code; an ADR and three document edits. Buys: the one claim in the product a risk quant would call indefensible, removed.
- Alternative: keep the wording. Cost: nothing to build and a question nobody can answer in the demo.

---

## 6. What I did not check

- **I made no network call.** I do not know whether a Polymarket contract matching M1 exists today — hence D3. The recorded-quote design is deliberately robust to it not existing, but the demo's headline is not.
- **I did not run the frontend, Playwright, `make eval`, or anything that calls a model or costs money**, per the common brief.
- **I did not re-run the strike-branch numbers myself** (`apply` is not exported from `domain/branch.py` under that name and I stopped rather than hunt). I relied on `spec/multiverse/propagation.md:456`, which records the engine's own `.46 → .41` and `.43 → .36`.
- **I did not measure** how long a 20 000-draw daily path simulation takes over the Hormuz map. I estimate milliseconds in numpy over a `(20000, 45)` float array, but I did not run it. If it is slow, the draw count is the knob.
- **I did not verify** that the engine's `truth` array is still shaped `(versions, worlds, days)` end-to-end under every branch — I read `propagation.py:1444-1463` and confirmed the assignment, not the full lifetime.
- **I did not read** audit-G (generation) or audit-H (UX) in full, only their finance-adjacent rows; ENGINE, GENERATION and UX analysts cover those.
- **I did not price** the browser work beyond a line estimate; audit-H's dock placement is assumed correct without my checking the Inspector's section stack myself.
- **Calibration is untested and stays untested.** Nothing in this design validates that the model's probabilities are any good. The card says so; that is all it can honestly do.

103	(~$4, ~40 min) plus a cassette re-record (~$1). So they go in **one commit, once**:
104	
105	```python
106	class LinkDraft(BaseModel):
107	    mode: Literal["trigger", "sustain"]
108	    p_effect_if_cause: float      # P(effect | cause), plain probability
109	    p_effect_if_not_cause: float  # P(effect | not cause)
110	    lag: int
111	    shape: Literal["impulse", "step", "ramp"]
112	    half_life: int | None = None
113	    rationale: str
114	    what_would_change_my_mind: str     # one named observable
115	    sources: tuple[SourceDraft, ...] = ()
116	
117	class SourceDraft(BaseModel):
118	    url: str
119	    quote: str   # the sentence on that page that carries the weight
120	    role: Literal["mechanism", "magnitude", "timing", "resolution", "instrument"]
121	```
122	
123	Our code keeps every decision it already owns: it mints ids, stamps `owner="model"`, computes
124	`strength = logit(q₁) − logit(q₀)` (clipped, with the clip reported), sets the leak to `q₀`, decides
125	`documented`/`argued` from what the search returned, and now also records whether the quote's page was
126	reachable. **Removed**: `strength` as an elicited field, and with it the "+1 triples the odds" anchor.
127	Also in the freeze: `kind` required on both payoff shapes (the branch already written); the three
128	inhibitor/falsifier sentences; the "do not search on the first call" rule; the thin-base-rate rule.
129	
130	**Then, and only then, re-record Hormuz once.** Everything else waits behind it.
131	
132	### 2.2 Latency, bought cheaply
133	
134	Two changes, measured, ~40 lines: the starting call does not search (**7 s** to the first tile,
135	measured) and `at_once` goes 3 → 5 (measured parallelism is already 1.5× at 3). At `EFFORT=medium`
136	that is a first tile at ~15 s and a whole map in ~5 minutes for $1.31 — which is what a live user
137	gets. The recordings stay at default effort (G13 stands).
138	
139	### 2.3 Skeleton-first: a bet, not a premise (stack 06)
140	
141	Its quality argument is measurably dead — the walk already draws DAGs with up to four parents. Its
142	remaining case is **more map per minute** and a first tile that arrives while a human is still
143	reading the hypothesis. Priced against the measurements, not the sketch: **≈$2.0–2.6 and ≈5–6
144	minutes** for 15–18 claims, first tile ~20 s *and only if we build a streaming JSON path that does
145	not exist today*. Compare: today's medium-effort run with §2.2's fixes is ~5 minutes and $1.31 for
146	9–12 claims. So it buys size and first-paint, not wall clock, for about twice the money and 2.5–3
147	sessions.
148	
149	Build it as **one decision per proposal, with proposals arriving in batches** — `grow.py` stays the
150	one walk driver, each element in the skeleton folds through the same `_judge` on the same candidate
151	map, and each emits the same `proposal_accepted` / `proposal_rejected` with a rising `at`, so the
152	recording grammar, replay and reject-never-repair all survive untouched. Amends ADR-0006's *"one
153	call per proposal"* to *"one decision per proposal"*. **Kill criterion, decided on the scorecard:**
154	if a skeleton round does not beat the walk on `claims`, `inhibiting_links` and `source_support_rate`
155	at equal or lower dollars, it is deleted and the walk stands.
156	
157	### 2.4 Evidence (stack 05, with the fetch-check in 06)
158	
159	The smallest change that gets most of the value is the two fields above plus an Inspector that reads
160	*quote → role → link*, and **the showcase's trade-critical sources checked by hand once** — which is
161	what both reviews actually ask for. Review2's automatic check cannot be built: the service returns
162	`encrypted_content`, not text, and the structured answer carries no `citations`. The honest automatic
163	version is **our own** fetch of the cited page and a substring match — the same shape of rule as
164	`keep_cited`, and a fourth word a reader can trust. It belongs in 06 because it adds a network step
165	to generation that replay must never need.
166	
167	### 2.5 Evaluation (counts in 05, rubric in 07)
168	
169	Add the seven counting columns to the existing scorecard — they cost nothing and they are exactly the
170	properties that changed between 09-17 and today, so they are what a regression would show. Keep the
171	house rule that **no model grades a model**. The content questions both reviews want are graded by
172	**a person, once per round**, on a printed sheet of 10 maps × 6 axes: resolvable · mechanism specific
173	· source supports the claim · DAG not tree · priced-in named · observation versus intervention. One
174	afternoon. Put it in stack 07 beside the pastcast — and **prefer the rubric to the pastcast**: the
175	pastcast needs a date-frozen corpus we do not have, and review/ 10:31 warns that a binary Brier score
176	cannot validate an interval over a latent probability anyway. The rubric is the cheaper instrument
177	and it answers the question Kent actually has.
178	
179	### 2.6 Interactive verbs (stack 06) — and what stack 06 is now FOR
180	
181	Stack 06 stops being "probes" and becomes **the map you can argue with**: *expand this claim* ·
182	*challenge this arrow* · *add an event* (built, one live run from proven), ranked by *spend here*
183	(already computed). *Challenge this arrow* **is** the role-played expert FR-9 permits and the red-team
184	call review2 wants — one feature where the roadmap had two. Cut: `refine`/INV-10, reflexive-loop
185	unrolling, the random-simulation probe.
186	
187	**Records amended:** ADR-0006 (one *decision* per proposal; the research budget narrowed), ADR-0003's
188	2026-09-17 amendment (unchanged — three silent retries stand), ADR-0015 (the coherence residual now;
189	k = 3 only if the scorecard earns it; G1's *"nothing extra in a recording"* is what an ensemble would
190	break, and it must be said out loud), ADR-0010 (a source carries a passage and a role), ADR-0013
191	(`kind` required). PRD anti-pattern 2 gains one clarifying clause.
192	
193	---
194	
195	## 3. Where the two reviews disagree, and who is right
196	
197	| Question | review/ | review2 | Who is right |
198	|---|---|---|---|
199	| When to abandon one-proposal-per-call | **Test it** now against the current design, and *"do not assume batching wins merely because it uses fewer calls"* (08:192) | **Skeleton-first wins, and it wins on quality before it wins on speed** (§7.1) | **review/.** Its caution is now a measured fact: the quality premise (a single call is the only way to get a second parent) is false — the walk produced 7 cross-links and 3 inhibitors without it. review2 is still right that it is the fastest route to a first tile. Verdict: build it, gated, in 06 |
200	| Latency targets | refuses to name one; demands both numbers be measured (08:188) | 2.5–3.5 min, ≈$0.70 | **review/ on method, review2 on ambition.** review2's numbers are ~2× (time) and ~3× (cost) optimistic against the measured $0.139/call and 55 tok/s |
201	| The evidence fix | *attach the passage, its support role, and why it is relevant*; **a human checks the showcase's sources** (10:30, 10:110) | one `quote` field, substring-checked against the search result's snippet | **review/.** review2's mechanism cannot run — there is no snippet, only `encrypted_content`. review/'s support-role enum is the part with real teeth |
202	| Evaluation | 8–12 cases; **08** names the *review fields*, **10** names the *case inventory*; explicitly human, not a model score | counts plus a 10-hypothesis, 6-axis hand rubric | **Both, and they are complementary.** Build the table with 10's case list and 08's field list; review2 supplies the counting columns |
203	| Pastcast | 08 calls its absence a calibration gap; 10 keeps it as a *later* diagnostic with a statistical warning; 04 cuts backtesting outright | silent | **10.** And on the brief's question: the rubric beats the pastcast on value per unit of work |
204	| `refine` / probes / loops | defer everything not in the loop (08:321, 10:112) | cut from v1 | **Agree — cut.** Deferring a thing with an invariant attached leaves a claim in the definition of done that is not true |
205	| Use case 1 | never mentions backward search; wants *route + weakest assumption + "no supported path within these limits"* | backward expansion for 2 layers, `LinkProposal` closes the middle | **review2**, and it is cheaper than it sounds — the backward machinery already exists in `add_a_claim` + `expand_toward` |
206	
207	---
208	
209	## 4. What changes for the branches in flight
210	
211	| Branch | Change | Why |
212	|---|---|---|
213	| `feat/04b-recordings` (Hormuz, `1c224cc…`) | **KEEP AND LAND AS IT IS. Do not re-record.** | It is the only keyless demo that exists, it cost $4 and 36 minutes, and it is sound. Re-recording now pays for a fingerprint that stack 05 will move again within days |
214	| `fix/04-payoff-kind-required` | **HOLD, do not land yet.** Rebase it onto the stack-05 shape-freeze commit and land them together. **Release the held cassette re-record** — it too waits for the freeze | This directly answers the coordinator's open question. The defect is **latent, not biting**: the model emitted `kind` on all 11 payoffs in the recording anyway. Landing it alone buys nothing and costs a $4 + 40-minute re-record that stack 05 immediately invalidates. **Pay once** |
215	| `feat/04b-evals` | **Land items 1–2. Add G-t (a round-level spending total, ~15 lines) before it lands.** Keep the path product on hold — both reviews call it invalid and ENGINE owns the replacement. Add the seven counting columns in 05, not now | A $15 intent that can spend $60 is exactly the kind of quiet untruth this repository refuses elsewhere |
216	| `feat/04a-growth` | **No change from me.** Its growth screen is what makes the latency work visible; note for it that the first tile will move from ~67 s to ~15 s after 05 | — |
217	| `fix/04-vanishing-wire` | No change. | — |
218	| **New, small, free of the fingerprint (NOW):** G-q (refusal says *by our rules* or *by the answer*), G-r (dropped sources and dropped base rates reach the wire), G-i (one clause on anti-pattern 2) | ~90 lines, 0.5 session | None of these touch `STANDING_TEXT` or `what_goes_out()`, so none of them costs a recording |
219	
220	---
221	
222	## 5. The generation parts of stacks 05, 06 and 07 — as a plan
223	
224	### Stack 05 — *the shapes settle, and the map earns its evidence* (generation share: ~2.5 sessions)
225	
226	| Order | Work | Lines | Cost |
227	|---|---|---|---|
228	| 05-G0 | **The shape freeze, one commit**: conditional numbers on the arrow (G-c, G-d) · `quote` + `role` on a source (G-e) · `kind` required on both payoffs (the held branch) · three inhibitor/falsifier sentences in `STANDING_TEXT` (G-b) · no search on the first call and `at_once` 5 (G-g) · research a base rate only where one can exist, and drop `n < 5` (G-j) · the payoff-instrument validator rule (G-o) | +430 −70 | 1.2 sess |
229	| 05-G1 | **One paid re-record of Hormuz** at default effort, plus the cassettes | — | ~$5, ~45 min, coordinator only |
230	| 05-G2 | **The coherence residual** — computed, shown, no extra call (G-w) | +40 | 0.2 sess |
231	| 05-G3 | **Verify becomes a real search** — a backward frontier from the destination using `add_a_claim` + `expand_toward`; *supported / fragile / no supported route within these limits* (G-u) | +180 | 0.7 sess |
232	| 05-G4 | **Seven counting columns** on the scorecard (G-s, G-m, G-n) | +90 | 0.3 sess |
233	| **Not done in 05, and why** | skeleton-first (needs a streaming path and a measured baseline to beat); any ensemble (nothing to compare it against yet); the fetch-check (a network step in generation); the three other recordings (**Kent's standing instruction**) | | |
234	
235	### Stack 06 — *the map you can argue with* (generation share: ~4 sessions)
236	
237	| Order | Work | Lines | Cost |
238	|---|---|---|---|
239	| 06-G1 | **Expand this claim** — `POST /api/generate/expand {base_id, branch, proposition_id}` over the existing `expand()`. The direct repair for an amputated headline branch | +130 | 0.5 sess |
240	| 06-G2 | **Challenge this arrow** — one call returns the strongest counter-argument, one inhibiting claim and a source, validated as an ordinary proposal. This *is* FR-9's role-played expert and review2's red team | +260 | 1.0 sess |
241	| 06-G3 | **Add an event** — wire up the built path; one live run to prove it | +40 | 0.3 sess |
242	| 06-G4 | **Spend here** — a route and the Inspector sentence for `World.range_shares`, with review/'s caveat on screen | +130 | 0.7 sess |
243	| 06-G5 | **Skeleton-first, gated.** One streamed structured call drafts a *thin* skeleton (sentence · kind · arrows), enrichment in parallel per element, one red-team call. Batched proposals, one decision each, same `_judge`, same events. **Kill criterion on the scorecard** | +650 −200 | 2.5–3 sess |
244	| 06-G6 | **The fetch-and-substring check** on cited pages (G-e fuller) | +120 | 0.5 sess |
245	| **Not done in 06, and why** | `refine` + INV-10 (**CUT** — more detail need not preserve the marginal; the invariant is satisfied by a named refusal) · reflexive-loop unrolling (**CUT** — a simulation law the assignment does not ask for) · the random-simulation probe (**CUT** — the band already comes from the engine) · autonomous agent society (anti-pattern 7) | | |
246	
247	### Stack 07 — *how we know a map is any good* (generation share: ~1.5 sessions + human time)
248	
249	| Order | Work | Cost |
250	|---|---|---|
251	| 07-G1 | **The hand rubric** — 10 hypotheses (the brief's four plus six the prompt has never seen) × 6 axes, scored 0–2 by a person on a printed sheet, notes kept beside each saved case. Built once, run per round | 0.4 sess + **one human afternoon per round**, ~$5–20 of model spend per round |
252	| 07-G2 | **The ensemble decision, on numbers** — k = 3 on the arrows into tradeable endings only, geometric mean of odds, **the raw samples kept in the recording**, judged on the rubric and the counting columns against the 05 baseline. Reject if flat | 0.7 sess, ~$1–2 a round |
253	| 07-G3 | **The other three recordings** — only on Kent's explicit word | ~$15, ~2 h |
254	| 07-G4 | Pastcast — **only if appetite remains after the rubric.** It needs a date-frozen corpus that does not exist, and a Brier score on a binary outcome cannot validate an interval over a latent probability | 1.5+ sess |
255	| **Not done, and why** | a model grading a model (Kent vetoes it, and both reviews agree the rubric must be human) · calibration fitting (nothing has resolved) · extremizing (research-A: LLM samples are correlated; it manufactures confidence) | |
256	
257	---
258	
259	## 6. Decisions that are genuinely Kent's
260	
261	**1. The Hormuz re-recording: wait, or pay twice.** *(recommended first)*
262	
263	> Your Hormuz recording cost $4 and 36 minutes. Making the payoff `kind` required changes what we ask
264	> the model for, so the recording no longer matches what ships and the build says to record it again.
265	> Stack 05 will change what we ask for a second time — conditional numbers on the arrows, a quoted
266	> passage on every source. **Recommendation: land the recording you already have, hold the payoff fix
267	> and the cassette re-record until all the shape changes land together, then record once.** Cost:
268	> $0 now, ~$5 and ~45 minutes once, in stack 05. The alternative — record now and again later — is
269	> ~$10 and ~90 minutes for the same result. There is no risk in waiting: the payoff defect is latent
270	> (the model filled the field anyway in all eleven of the recording's trades).
271	
272	**2. The number on an arrow becomes two probabilities.**
273	
274	> Today the model writes an abstract "strength", and the description we send it says "+1 triples the
275	> odds" — a number we invented, in a prompt. Instead we ask two plain questions: *how likely is the
276	> effect if the cause happens?* and *how likely if it does not?* Our code turns those into the same
277	> arrow. On screen the Inspector stops saying "strength 2.2" and starts saying, in this shape,
278	> **"war-risk premiums falling takes Brent below $68 from *this* to *that*"** — the two numbers read
279	> off the arrow rather than invented here — a sentence a trader can disagree with. It also
280	> gives us a free honesty check: the model's three numbers around each arrow must roughly agree, and
281	> we can show by how much they do not. Cost: ~0.7 session and it rides the one re-record above.
282	> Option B: keep `strength` and only bound it. Cheaper by half a session; keeps the anchor we wrote.
283	
284	**3. Skeleton-first is a bet with a kill switch, not a foregone conclusion.**
285	
286	> The review said drawing the whole map in one call is the *only* way to get a claim with two causes.
287	> Measured on your own recording, that is no longer true: the map already has claims with two and
288	> four causes, and the run before the recording drew three arrows that push *down*. What one big call
289	> would still buy is a first tile in about twenty seconds instead of a minute or two, and a bigger
290	> map for the same wait. Priced honestly it is about **$2.0–2.6 and five to six minutes** — roughly
291	> twice today's money at medium effort — and 2.5–3 sessions of work including a streaming path we do
292	> not have. **Recommendation: buy the cheap 90% first** (the first call does not search — measured at
293	> 7 seconds — and five lines grow at once), then build the big call in stack 06 and delete it if it
294	> does not beat the walk on the scorecard. Option B: build it in 05, before the thesis. It is the one
295	> thing here that could eat a week.
296	
297	**4. Twenty-five searches a claim: keep, narrow, or drop.**
298	
299	> You decided the model should research its reference class, up to 25 searches a claim. Measured:
300	> 93 searches on the Hormuz recording produced **five** base rates across eighteen claims, and three
301	> of those five are "0 out of 2", "2 out of 3" and "1 out of 1" — which are not reference classes.
302	> A call that searches takes three to four times as long as one that does not, so this is where most
303	> of the thirty-six minutes went. **Recommendation: research only where a reference class can exist**
304	> — not on the first call, not on a price threshold — and drop a count with fewer than five cases
305	> rather than print "1 of 1". Cost: ~0.3 session; saves roughly a third of the clock.
306	
307	**5. Who grades quality — and is a rubric better value than a pastcast?**
308	
309	> Today's evals count shapes: no loops, every arrow has a reason, every trade names an instrument.
310	> They cannot see that a source does not say what we cite it for. **Recommendation: you, or one
311	> person, once a round** — ten maps, six questions each, on one printed page, one afternoon. No model
312	> ever grades another model. That is worth more than the pastcast in stack 07, which needs a corpus
313	> frozen before each event that we do not have, and whose score cannot actually test the thing we
314	> would want tested. Cost: half a session to build, one afternoon per round. Option B: pastcast
315	> first — a stronger public claim if it works, one-and-a-half sessions plus the corpus problem.
316	
317	**6. Stack 06 changes what it is for.**
318	
319	> It was "probes": split a claim into finer claims, run simulations on one node, role-play experts,
320	> unroll feedback loops. Both reviews say cut all of that. **Recommendation: stack 06 becomes the map
321	> you can argue with** — *expand this claim*, *challenge this arrow*, *add an event*, each ranked by
322	> the "spend here" number the engine already computes and nobody can see. The role-played expert
323	> survives as *challenge this arrow*, which is the honest version of it. What that costs you: the
324	> chess-engine analogy you liked. What it buys: the brief's audit clause, and the one inhibiting
325	> arrow the showcase map does not have.
326	
327	---
328	
329	## 7. What I did not check
330	
331	- **I did not call a model or spend a cent**, so every latency and cost figure for anything not yet
332	  built is arithmetic over the measured runs, not a measurement. In particular the skeleton-first
333	  numbers (≈$2.0–2.6, ≈5–6 min, ~20 s first tile) rest on the measured 55 output-tokens/second and
334	  $0.139/call, and on a guess at how many tokens a thin skeleton is. A one-call spike would settle it
335	  for about $0.20.
336	- **I did not run the test suites, the browser, or `make eval`.** The evals findings come from
337	  reading `evals/run.py` and `spec/generation/evaluation.md` on `feat/04b-evals`, not from a round.
338	- **I did not verify that a streaming structured call can be recorded by the cassette layer.** VCR
339	  and streamed responses are awkward together; that is unquantified risk on 06-G5.
340	- **I did not check any source in any map by hand.** The claim that the recording's evidence is thin
341	  rests on the shape of `Source` (url, title, date — no passage), not on opening thirty-seven pages.
342	  Checking the trade-critical ones is itself one of my recommendations.
343	- **I did not read the frontend Inspector code**, so my line estimates for its changes (~40–80 lines
344	  each) are the weakest numbers here. CRAFT owns that surface.
345	- **I did not price the rate-limit risk** of running 12–37 enrichment calls concurrently against the
346	  service.
347	- **The engine's two reproduced defects are ENGINE's**, not mine; I assumed their fixes land and do
348	  not change the generation shapes. If the engine's reformulation changes what an arrow *is*, my
349	  "freeze the shapes once" plan absorbs it — but only if it lands before 05-G1.

# Digest — GENERATION

**2026-09-21 · read-only analyst · lens: how the model draws a map, what evidence it attaches, and how we know a map is any good.**

No repository file was changed. Everything below that says *measured* was computed by a script in
`/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kentgang-git3-katalyst/b70a1857-a894-4bbe-b3a6-4d7cf3ebc4f8/scratchpad/digest/generation/`
(`measure.py`, `timing.py`) over the one committed recording
(`katalyst-wt/feat-04b-recordings/backend/recordings/hormuz.jsonl`) and the three kept runs under
`backend/.runs/`. No model was called and no money was spent.

---

## 0. The measurements, first

Both reviewers read the run of **2026-09-17** (10 claims, 9 arrows, a pure tree). Much has changed.
Here is what the artefacts say **today**.

| | 09-17 opus | 09-21 sonnet, default | 09-21 sonnet, medium | **the committed recording** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claims / arrows | 10 / 9 | 20 / 26 | 9 / 10 | **18 / 19** |
| `links / (claims−1)` | **1.00** (pure tree) | **1.37** | 1.25 | **1.12** |
| Claims with >1 parent | 0 | 5 (one has 4) | 2 | **2** |
| Cross-links (2nd incoming arrow) | 0 | 7 | 2 | **2** |
| Arrows that push DOWN (inhibitors) | 0 | **3** | 0 | **0** |
| Arrows pushing down into an ending (falsifiers) | 0 | 1 | 0 | **0** |
| Max depth | 3 | 5 | 3 | **3** |
| Endings as a share of claims | 70% | 45% | 56% | **61%** |
| Base rates kept | 8/10 (0 sourced) | 10/20 | 2/9 | **5/18** |
| …of those, `n ≤ 5` | 0 | **7** | 1 | **3** (`0/2`, `2/3`, `1/1`) |
| Distinct payoff instruments | 7 of 7 | 7 of 9 | 5 of 5 | **11 of 11** |
| Narrating claims (`^With|Once|After…`) | 9/10 | 0/20 | 0/9 | **0/18** |
| Calls · searches · dollars · wall clock | 10 · 9 · $1.32 · 10m54 | 34 · 108 · $4.89 · 44m33 | 17 · 38 · $1.31 · 7m46 | **29 · 93 · $4.04 · 36m19** |
| Dollars per call | $0.132 | $0.144 | $0.077 | **$0.139** |
| **Seconds to the FIRST tile** | **7 s** (no search) | **135 s** | **67 s** | not timed per call |
| **Seconds to a first complete chain** (hypothesis → ending, scaled by the run's measured parallelism) | **151 s** | **611 s** | **95 s** | — |
| Parallelism actually achieved (`Σ per-call ÷ wall clock`) | 1.00× | **1.51×** | 1.49× | — |

Four measured facts that change the argument:

1. **The map is no longer a tree.** `LinkProposal` — the shape review2 says is never used — is used in
   **2 of 20** accepted proposals in the recording and **7 of 28** in the 09-21 default run, and those
   are exactly the cross-links. The claim that *"`ClaimProposal`'s single `cause` field is why the
   measured map is a pure tree"* was true of the 09-17 run and is **false today**.
2. **A call that searches costs 3–4× the seconds of one that does not.** Default effort: median
   **101 s** searching versus **26 s** not. Medium effort: **50 s** versus **15 s**. Search is the
   clock, and 79% / 63% of written tokens are thinking.
3. **G7's research budget bought thin reference classes.** 93 searches produced **5** base rates on 18
   claims, and **3 of those 5 are `0/2`, `2/3`, `1/1`** — not reference classes. The 09-21 default run:
   108 searches, 10 base rates, **7 of them `n ≤ 5`**.
4. **The model can draw inhibitors when it is asked something adversarial.** The recording's own
   scripted insert (*"…but Iran is struck the next day"*) produced **three arrows, all negative**
   (−1.8, −1.1, −1.6). The walk's standing prompt never contains the words *inhibit*, *falsify*,
   *blocker* or *parents* — grep across `engine/` and `domain/` returns nothing. The map is rosy
   because nobody asks it not to be, not because the shapes forbid it.

---

## 1. The findings table

Verdicts: **NOW** (stack-04 tail) · **05** · **06** · **07** · **CUT** · **REJECT**.
Cost: sessions of ~3 focused hours, and rough lines added/deleted.

| # | Finding | Who | Status today (evidence) | Cost if left | Cheapest honest fix | Fuller fix | Cost | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **G-a** | The map is a pure tree; no common causes; `LinkProposal` never used | review2 G-2, §7.1 | **NEVER TRUE / FIXED SINCE.** Measured: 1.12–1.37 links per claim; 2 and 7 `LinkProposal` accepts; one claim has 4 parents | — | nothing | nothing | 0 | **REJECT** — and the main *quality* argument for skeleton-first goes with it |
| **G-b** | No inhibiting arrows anywhere; a geopolitical map that is all good news | review2 G-2 | **PARTLY.** 3 inhibitors in the 09-21 default run, **0 in the recording**, 0 falsifiers into an ending. ## 2. The design I recommend

**One sentence: freeze the answer shapes once, record once, buy the latency cheaply, and make
skeleton-first a measured bet in stack 06 rather than an article of faith.**

### 2.1 The shape freeze (stack 05, top)

Everything that changes `STANDING_TEXT` or `what_goes_out()` moves the prompt fingerprint
(`prompt.py:154`), and a moved fingerprint fails `check_recordings` and costs a paid re-record
(~$4, ~40 min) plus a cassette re-record (~$1). So they go in **one commit, once**:

```python
class LinkDraft(BaseModel):
    mode: Literal["trigger", "sustain"]
    p_effect_if_cause: float      # P(effect | cause), plain probability
    p_effect_if_not_cause: float  # P(effect | not cause)
    lag: int
    shape: Literal["impulse", "step", "ramp"]
    half_life: int | None = None
    rationale: str
    what_would_change_my_mind: str     # one named observable
    sources: tuple[SourceDraft, ...] = ()

class SourceDraft(BaseModel):
    url: str
    quote: str   # the sentence on that page that carries the weight
    role: Literal["mechanism", "magnitude", "timing", "resolution", "instrument"]
```

Our code keeps every decision it already owns: it mints ids, stamps `owner="model"`, computes
`strength = logit(q₁) − logit(q₀)` (clipped, with the clip reported), sets the leak to `q₀`, decides
`documented`/`argued` from what the search returned, and now also records whether the quote's page was
reachable. **Removed**: `strength` as an elicited field, and with it the "+1 triples the odds" anchor.
Also in the freeze: `kind` required on both payoff shapes (the branch already written); the three
inhibitor/falsifier sentences; the "do not search on the first call" rule; the thin-base-rate rule.

**Then, and only then, re-record Hormuz once.** Everything else waits behind it.

### 2.2 Latency, bought cheaply

Two changes, measured, ~40 lines: the starting call does not search (**7 s** to the first tile,
measured) and `at_once` goes 3 → 5 (measured parallelism is already 1.5× at 3). At `EFFORT=medium`
that is a first tile at ~15 s and a whole map in ~5 minutes for $1.31 — which is what a live user
gets. The recordings stay at default effort (G13 stands).

### 2.3 Skeleton-first: a bet, not a premise (stack 06)

Its quality argument is measurably dead — the walk already draws DAGs with up to four parents. Its
remaining case is **more map per minute** and a first tile that arrives while a human is still
reading the hypothesis. Priced against the measurements, not the sketch: **≈$2.0–2.6 and ≈5–6
minutes** for 15–18 claims, first tile ~20 s *and only if we build a streaming JSON path that does
not exist today*. Compare: today's medium-effort run with §2.2's fixes is ~5 minutes and $1.31 for
9–12 claims. So it buys size and first-paint, not wall clock, for about twice the money and 2.5–3
sessions.

Build it as **one decision per proposal, with proposals arriving in batches** — `grow.py` stays the
one walk driver, each element in the skeleton folds through the same `_judge` on the same candidate
map, and each emits the same `proposal_accepted` / `proposal_rejected` with a rising `at`, so the
recording grammar, replay and reject-never-repair all survive untouched. Amends ADR-0006's *"one
call per proposal"* to *"one decision per proposal"*. **Kill criterion, decided on the scorecard:**
if a skeleton round does not beat the walk on `claims`, `inhibiting_links` and `source_support_rate`
at equal or lower dollars, it is deleted and the walk stands.

### 2.4 Evidence (stack 05, with the fetch-check in 06)

The smallest change that gets most of the value is the two fields above plus an Inspector that reads
*quote → role → link*, and **the showcase's trade-critical sources checked by hand once** — which is
what both reviews actually ask for. Review2's automatic check cannot be built: the service returns
`encrypted_content`, not text, and the structured answer carries no `citations`. The honest automatic
version is **our own** fetch of the cited page and a substring match — the same shape of rule as
`keep_cited`, and a fourth word a reader can trust. It belongs in 06 because it adds a network step
to generation that replay must never need.

### 2.5 Evaluation (counts in 05, rubric in 07)

Add the seven counting columns to the existing scorecard — they cost nothing and they are exactly the
properties that changed between 09-17 and today, so they are what a regression would show. Keep the
house rule that **no model grades a model**. The content questions both reviews want are graded by
**a person, once per round**, on a printed sheet of 10 maps × 6 axes: resolvable · mechanism specific
· source supports the claim · DAG not tree · priced-in named · observation versus intervention. One
afternoon. Put it in stack 07 beside the pastcast — and **prefer the rubric to the pastcast**: the
pastcast needs a date-frozen corpus we do not have, and review/ 10:31 warns that a binary Brier score
cannot validate an interval over a latent probability anyway. The rubric is the cheaper instrument
and it answers the question Kent actually has.

### 2.6 Interactive verbs (stack 06) — and what stack 06 is now FOR

Stack 06 stops being "probes" and becomes **the map you can argue with**: *expand this claim* ·
*challenge this arrow* · *add an event* (built, one live run from proven), ranked by *spend here*
(already computed). *Challenge this arrow* **is** the role-played expert FR-9 permits and the red-team
call review2 wants — one feature where the roadmap had two. Cut: `refine`/INV-10, reflexive-loop
unrolling, the random-simulation probe.

**Records amended:** ADR-0006 (one *decision* per proposal; the research budget narrowed), ADR-0003's
2026-09-17 amendment (unchanged — three silent retries stand), ADR-0015 (the coherence residual now;
k = 3 only if the scorecard earns it; G1's *"nothing extra in a recording"* is what an ensemble would
break, and it must be said out loud), ADR-0010 (a source carries a passage and a role), ADR-0013
(`kind` required). PRD anti-pattern 2 gains one clarifying clause.

Both reproduce **unchanged** on this branch, so the spread neither creates nor masks either.

For a claim with **no causes** `total` is `broadcast(baseline)`, so `answer` is *identical in all eight worlds of a version*; `_per_version` then averages it over the surviving subset and gets exactly the same number back. Rao-Blackwellisation is exact for an *unconditional* mean, and invalid once you condition on another claim's realised outcome, because the conditioning event depends on the value that was discarded. The Bayes answer would come back by reading `came_true[A]` over the surviving worlds instead of `answer[A]`, at the cost of the variance reduction the whole band rests on — which is why this is a design decision and not a patch. It is the same phenomenon `diff.md` already records as G3's "moved only by reweighting", described there as a property rather than as a defect. **Interaction with the spread: none.** A has no incoming arrows, so no drawn push enters its baseline and its answer is still constant across worlds within a version. For a claim that *does* have causes, the answer already varies across worlds, the observation does reach it, and the spread only widens the band.

**2. `do(C)`/`do(R)` move B but move M1 and M2 by exactly 0.0000.** Root cause: `fired[claim_id] = came_true[:, :, starts]` where `starts = _point_of(points, setup.settled[claim_id])`. The two readings that would let later pushes through are "the day this arrow's own push fires" (`settled[source] + lag`) and "the source's own resolve-by day"; both change every recorded number, so this is Kent's call. **Interaction with the spread: none that can change the zero.** The spread varies `H→B`, `C→B` and `R→B`, so it changes the distribution of B's day-2 flag — but identically in the base world and the `do(C)` world, because C's arrow contributes nothing on day 2 in either. Reading the simulated outcome would give the Bayes answer, but it gives up the variance reduction the bands rest on. So this is a design decision for the engine plan, not a patch.
- **Endings ignore two of B's four causes.** A trigger arrow reads its source only on the day the source's earliest incoming arrow lands. B's earliest arrow lands on day 2. C's push lands on day 7 and R's on day 5, so they change B's own series but B's outgoing arrows never see them. The fix is choosing which day a trigger reads, and any choice changes every recorded number.
